opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and it came out of a frustration more than anything. For a long time, the dominant way to build world models in reinforcement learning was to train them on data from an agent interacting with an environment, so you always had the actions logged alongside the observations. That works well, but it limits you to whatever environments you can afford to collect data in, and those tend to be fairly narrow.

Meanwhile, there's this enormous amount of video on the internet: people playing games, robots doing things, people going about their lives. It contains a huge amount of information about how the world works and how agents affect it. The catch is that almost none of it comes with action labels. You see what happened, but you don't know which button was pressed or which motor command was sent.

So the question became: can we infer the actions ourselves? The intuition behind latent actions is quite simple. If you look at two consecutive frames, the change between them is partly explained by the environment's dynamics and partly by whatever the agent did. If you train a model to predict the next frame, but force the information about the agent's choice through a very small bottleneck, say a small discrete set of codes, the model learns to put the controllable part of the change into that bottleneck. Those codes end up behaving like actions, even though nobody ever told the model what an action was.

What made us excited was seeing that these learned latent actions were actually consistent and meaningful. The same code would move a character left across very different scenes, for example. That suggested you could get a controllable, interactive world model purely from watching videos, which really changes the scaling story. Instead of being limited by labeled interaction data, you're limited by how much video you can train on, and that's a much bigger pool.

There's also a nice side benefit: once you have a latent action space, you can potentially use it to train agents, by learning policies in that latent space and then mapping to real actions with a small amount of labeled data. So it felt like a path not just to better world models, but toward more general agents as well.

r001.rationale: It says interaction data must be collected in each environment, which limits models to environments where collection is affordable, and motivates learning actions from unlabeled videos.

r002.rationale: It describes learning world models from videos and later training policies in latent action space, but does not contrast this with using latent actions to imitate video behaviors.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. It really came out of a frustration more than a grand plan. When we started thinking seriously about world models, the obvious bottleneck was data. If you want a model that understands how actions change an environment, the standard recipe is to collect trajectories with actions attached, and that works beautifully in a simulator where you control everything. But the moment you look at the real world, or even at the enormous amount of gameplay footage people have uploaded over the years, you realize almost none of it comes with action labels. The videos are there, the dynamics are all baked into them, but the thing that makes them useful for control, the "what did the agent do between this frame and the next," is just missing.

So the question we kept circling back to was: do you actually need the labels? And the intuition that eventually won us over was that the visual change between two consecutive frames is itself a pretty strong signal about what happened. If a character moves left, the pixels tell you that. You don't need someone to have logged a key press. The idea with latent actions is to learn a small, discrete code that explains the transition from one frame to the next, and to make it a bottleneck so the model can't just memorize the whole future. If the code is forced to be low-dimensional, the most efficient thing for it to capture is the controllable part of the change, the bit the agent is responsible for, rather than all the background noise.

What really convinced me was seeing it work at even modest scale. Early on we weren't sure whether the latent space would be meaningful at all, or whether it would just latch onto something like camera motion or lighting. But when you train it this way on gameplay video and then poke at the latent codes, they end up corresponding to things a human would recognize: move left, move right, jump, stay still. They're consistent across very different games, which was a bit surprising. And once you have that, you've effectively turned a passive video dataset into an interactive one. You can condition a dynamics model on those codes and start stepping through the world yourself.

The other thing that appealed to me is how well it fits the broader lesson from language and vision, which is that scale plus a simple self-supervised objective tends to beat clever but narrow supervision. Action labels are expensive and environment specific. Video is abundant and generic. If latent action learning lets you ride the same scaling curve that text models rode, then it stops being a trick and starts looking like the natural way to build world models. That's roughly the moment it went from an interesting side idea to something I thought was worth betting on.

r001.rationale: The response cites missing action labels in real-world and gameplay videos, but does not identify the lack of labeled interaction data for newly generated target environments.

r002.rationale: It describes using latent codes to model transitions and step through a world, but does not contrast this with using latent actions to imitate behaviors from videos.

astra-6.text:
The motivation was really the gap between the data we have and the data we typically need to learn a world model. There’s a huge amount of video showing how the world changes, but it generally doesn’t come with action labels. You can watch something happen without knowing what input caused it.

So the question becomes: can we learn a useful representation of those actions directly from the video? If you look at two successive frames, you can try to infer a latent variable that captures the transition, and then train a model to predict what happens next conditioned on that variable.

What makes that exciting is the possibility of turning passive video into something you can interact with. At generation time, you choose the latent action rather than infer it from the next frame. You don’t necessarily get a neatly labeled action like ‘move left’ automatically, and separating actions from other changes in the scene is a real challenge. But it gives you a way to learn controllable dynamics without requiring action annotations for every video.

r001.rationale: The response says videos generally lack action labels, but does not identify the lack of labeled interaction data for newly generated target environments as the motivation.

r002.rationale: It describes learning controllable dynamics and world models from videos, but does not contrast this with using latent actions to imitate behaviors from videos.

sol-6.1.text:
The appeal was really the gap between the video data we have and the data we typically use to train an interactive model. With video, you can observe how a scene changes, but you generally don’t have the actions that caused those changes. If you want a world model you can control, that missing action information is a big obstacle.

Latent action learning gives you a way to ask: can we infer a compact representation of what happened between two frames, and use that as the action signal? You train the model to predict what comes next, conditioned on that inferred action. Then the interesting question is whether those latent actions capture something consistent enough that you can select them yourself and steer the model.

That was what made it promising to me: the possibility of learning from video without action labels, while still getting something interactive. Predicting a plausible continuation is useful, but being able to influence that continuation is what starts to make it a world model you can use for decision-making.

r001.rationale: It notes that videos generally lack action labels, but does not identify the lack of labeled interaction data for newly generated target environments as the motivation.

r002.rationale: It describes learning controllable world models from video, but does not contrast that use with imitating behaviors from video.
